name: Republic of China
summary: Founded in 1912 after the last emperor abdicated. It governed mainland China until 1949, through warlord rule, Japanese invasion and civil war. Since 1949 its government has been based in Taiwan.

knownFor.label: Three Principles of the People
knownFor.note: Sun Yat-sen’s ideas of nationalism, democracy and people’s livelihood.

knownFor.label: Qipao (cheongsam)
knownFor.note: A dress that became fashionable in 1920s Shanghai.

location.value: Mainland China (1912–1949), with capitals at Beijing (1912–28) and Nanjing (1928–49), and wartime capitals Wuhan and Chongqing. Since 1949 its government has been based in Taiwan.

terrain.value: All of China’s varied geography, from the coastal plains to Tibet and Xinjiang (where central control was often weak).
terrain.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

climate.value: Varied. Famines struck repeatedly (e.g. the Henan famine of 1942–43).
climate.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

resources.value: Agriculture, and industry concentrated in coastal treaty ports such as Shanghai.
resources.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

disasters.value: Yellow River and Yangtze floods (1931), the Henan famine (1942–43), and the deliberate breaching of the Yellow River dikes (1938).
disasters.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

urbanisation.value: Shanghai was the largest city and a major global port.

disease.value: Epidemics during war and famine. Japan’s Unit 731 conducted biological warfare.
disease.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

migration.value: Tens of millions of refugees fled during the Japanese invasion. About 2 million people moved to Taiwan in 1949.
migration.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

economicBase.value: Mostly agricultural, with modern industry and banking in coastal cities (the “Nanjing decade” of 1927–37 saw growth).
economicBase.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

tradeRoutes.value: Foreign trade through treaty ports, dominated by Western and Japanese firms.
tradeRoutes.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

wealth.value: No GDP figure is given in the sources checked.

moneyAndTax.value: Silver dollars, then the fiat “national currency” (1935), then the gold yuan (1948), which collapsed in hyperinflation.

inequality.value: Landlords and peasants, and coastal wealth versus rural poverty, which helped the Communists win rural support.
inequality.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

governmentType.value: A republic: the Beiyang government (1912–28), then a one-party Nationalist (Kuomintang) state under Chiang Kai-shek. A constitution was adopted in 1947/48.

keyRulers.value: Sun Yat-sen (provisional president 1912). Yuan Shikai (1912–1916, briefly declared himself emperor). Chiang Kai-shek (Nationalist leader from 1928).

succession.value: Unstable: presidents were chosen by warlord factions or the Nationalist Party rather than by free elections.
succession.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

institutions.value: The Nationalist Party-state, the Five-Yuan system, and the 1947 constitution.
institutions.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

stability.value: The Warlord Era (1916–28), the Northern Expedition (1926–28), the Shanghai massacre of Communists (1927), and civil war with the Communists (1927–49).

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between warlords, the Nationalists and Communists, and factions within the Nationalist Party.
eliteConflict.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

armyAndTech.value: The Nationalist army (with German and later US advisers), plus regional warlord armies.
armyAndTech.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

majorWars.value: The Northern Expedition. The Japanese invasion of Manchuria (1931). The Second Sino-Japanese War (1937–45). The Chinese Civil War (to 1949).

territoryChange.value: Lost Manchuria to Japan (1931) and much of eastern China in the war. Recovered Taiwan in 1945. Lost the mainland to the Communists in 1949.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: Japan and the Communists. Allies: the US and Britain in the Second World War. A founding member of the UN Security Council (1945).
alliancesRivals.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

inventions.value: Modern universities, railways and industry developed in coastal areas.
inventions.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

scienceEducation.value: The New Culture and May Fourth movements (1915–1919) promoted science, democracy and vernacular writing.
scienceEducation.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

openness.value: Very open to Western ideas in the 1910s–20s.
openness.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

communicationTransport.value: Railways and roads expanded in the 1930s; in Taiwan, high-speed rail (2007).

religion.value: Confucian, Buddhist, Daoist and folk traditions, Christianity, and Islam. Many reformers were critical of tradition.
religion.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

languageWriting.value: Chinese. The vernacular written language (baihua) spread after 1919, and a national spoken standard (Mandarin) was promoted.
languageWriting.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

artsArchitecture.value: Modern literature (Lu Xun), Shanghai cinema, and Western-style architecture in Shanghai.
artsArchitecture.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

socialStructure.value: Landlords, peasants, new urban workers and a middle class. Changing roles for women (the end of foot-binding).
socialStructure.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

sharedIdentity.value: Chinese nationalism (Sun Yat-sen’s Three Principles of the People) in response to foreign encroachment.
sharedIdentity.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

dailyLife.value: In mainland China before 1949, mostly rural houses; in Taiwan today, city apartments; rice, noodles and night markets.

neighbours.value: Japan, the Soviet Union, Mongolia, British India and French Indochina.
neighbours.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

ideasReligions.value: Nationalism, liberalism and communism (the Communist Party was founded in 1921) shaped modern China.
ideasReligions.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

colonisation.value: Faced foreign concessions and Japanese occupation. Successfully pressed for the end of extraterritoriality (1943).
colonisation.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

riseSignals.value: The 1911 Revolution ended over 2,000 years of imperial rule. Reunification under the Nationalists (1928).

peakPeriod.value: The Nanjing decade (1927–1937), when the Nationalist government unified much of China.

declineSignals.value: Warlordism, the Japanese invasion, corruption, hyperinflation and loss of rural support.
declineSignals.source: Fenby, The Penguin History of Modern China (2019)

outcome.value: The Communists won the civil war and founded the PRC (1949). The ROC government retreated to Taiwan (7 December 1949), where it continues today. Taiwan’s political status is disputed: the PRC claims it, and the ROC governs it.

sources.value: Government and party archives, foreign diplomatic records and memoirs. Checked against Wikipedia (“Republic of China (1912–1949)”) on 6 Nov 2026. See also Fenby (2019).

overallCertainty.value: Good for events. Civil war death tolls and assessments of the Nationalist government are debated. This entry focuses on 1912–1949.

sources: Wikipedia: Republic of China (1912–1949) (infobox, checked 6 Nov 2026)
